feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Liquid potash weekly once flowering; balanced NPK fortnightly through spring.
sowingNotes: Sow on heat mat 20–25 °C. Prick out at first true leaf.
greenhouseNotes: Stake and single-leader prune. Vent above 28 °C.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Oct under cover; transplant once Papamoa night temps stay above 12 °C. String-train the leader and prune laterals weekly — coastal humidity makes airflow critical.

feedingNotes: Liquid potash weekly from first truss; switch to half-strength once cropping heavily to prevent splitting.
greenhouseNotes: Pinch laterals; allow side branching for cherry varieties.
growingNotes: Sow Jul–Nov on a heat mat; cherries set fruit faster than full-size tomatoes so a second sowing in Oct extends Papamoa harvest into May.

feedingNotes: Heaviest feeder of the tomatoes. Add compost + dolomite pre-plant, then liquid potash every 5–7 days once trusses set.
sowingNotes: Sow early — needs the longest season.
growingNotes: Sow Jul–Sep so plants are 25 cm tall by the time soil hits 16 °C in Papamoa. Keep to one leader and de-leaf below ripening trusses to deter humidity diseases.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed; liquid feed fortnightly. Avoid over-watering at ripening or fruit splits.
sowingNotes: Sauce variety; determinate types crop in concentrated flush.
growingNotes: Sow Jul–Oct. Determinate types crop all at once in late summer so block-plant 4–6 plants for a single sauce-making weekend.

feedingNotes: Light feeder until first fruit. Switch to potash-rich liquid feed every 10 days from late Nov.
greenhouseNotes: Stake; flowers drop above 32 °C — vent and shade Dec–Feb.
growingNotes: Sow Jul–Sep on heat mat; plant out under cover late Oct. Pinch the king flower for stronger early growth and shade-cloth the roof through Papamoa peak summer.

feedingNotes: Hold back nitrogen to push heat. Tomato food fortnightly once fruiting starts.
sowingNotes: Slow germinator. Start early on heat mat.
growingNotes: Sow Jul–Aug so plants are flowering by Dec. In a Papamoa greenhouse they overwinter — cut back hard in Jul and they'll fruit a second season.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich planting hole; liquid tomato food weekly once fruit sets.
greenhouseNotes: Heat lover; under glass through summer in BOP.
growingNotes: Sow Jul–Sep on heat mat; transplant only when soil is 18 °C. Stake plants and pinch growing tip after 6 fruit are set to size them up.

feedingNotes: Side-dress with compost mid-season; lighter feeder than tomato.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Oct and plant at least two seedlings — they will not self-pollinate. Cage like a tomato; in Papamoa they sprawl 1.5 m wide so leave room.

feedingNotes: Avoid heavy nitrogen — pushes leaf at the cost of fruit. Compost-rich soil and a single tomato-food top-up at flowering is enough.
greenhouseNotes: Perennial under glass; cut back hard in winter.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Oct, plant Oct–Dec. Under glass in Papamoa it carries on as a 3-year shrub — pick fruit from the ground once husks are papery.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Compost-mulch annually plus tomato food fortnightly while fruiting.
growingNotes: Plant cuttings Sep–Dec; trellis along the back wall of the greenhouse. Frost-free Papamoa winters mean it fruits year-round under glass.

feedingNotes: Balanced NPK fortnightly through summer. Excessive nitrogen delays podding.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Nov direct into 25 °C soil — won't germinate cold. In Papamoa it's a greenhouse-only crop; pick pods at 8 cm before they go fibrous.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich planting hole; liquid feed (high potash) weekly once flowering.
greenhouseNotes: Train up trellis; remove lower laterals.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Jan in modules at 25 °C. Single-leader train up strings under glass; for Papamoa humidity, snip off bottom 30 cm of leaves to prevent mildew.

feedingNotes: Same as cucumber — compost + weekly potash feed once flowering.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Jan; harvest at 5–7 cm every 1–2 days or plants stop producing. Bush varieties suit pots in a Papamoa greenhouse.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed at planting. Side-dress with sheep pellets at first flower; liquid feed fortnightly thereafter.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Jan direct outside, or two sowings under glass for an extended Papamoa harvest. Pick at 15 cm — daily checks once cropping.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed; weekly liquid feed once vines run. Reduce water at ripening to concentrate sugars.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Nov on heat mat; plant out when soil hits 20 °C. In Papamoa greenhouse, train vertically on netting and support fruit with stockings.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost-and-pellets at planting plus weekly liquid feed until fruit-set, then ease back.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Nov on heat mat. Choose icebox cultivars for Papamoa — full-size vines rarely get the heat-units needed under our marine cloud cover.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed. Weekly liquid feed until fruit half-grown then stop to ripen sweetly.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Nov; greenhouse-grown in Papamoa or you'll be racing autumn rain. Slip-test for ripeness — fruit detaches with light pressure.

feedingNotes: Compost-and-manure pre-plant; one mid-season liquid feed. Stop feeding once fruit are full-size to harden skins for storage.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Dec direct outdoors in Papamoa. Train along a fence to save bed space; cure picked fruit in the sun for 10 days for long winter storage.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich planting mound; liquid feed fortnightly until fruit are sized then stop.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Dec outdoors in Papamoa. Lift fruit onto a tile to keep the base dry — coastal humidity rots ground-side skin.

feedingNotes: Compost + sheep pellets pre-plant; mid-season liquid feed only.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Dec outdoors. Cure 10 days in sun after harvest then store frost-free — Papamoa-grown butternuts keep through to spring.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich mound; one mid-season liquid feed.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Dec. Vines sprawl 3 m so trellis or train along a fence in smaller Papamoa plots. Harvest when skin resists thumbnail pressure.

feedingNotes: Compost-and-pellets pre-plant; weekly liquid feed once cropping.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Dec outdoors. Pick young at 25 cm for tender flesh; left to mature they store like pumpkin through Papamoa winter.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed; weekly liquid feed all season — long-cropping plant.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Nov on heat mat; trellis along the greenhouse roof. Papamoa needs the full season under cover — leave fruit on vine until the skin is dry and rattles.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Diluted seaweed-and-fish liquid every 3 weeks keeps leaves green.
sowingNotes: Pinch tips weekly to keep bushy.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Feb; basil sulks in Papamoa night temps below 14 °C so wait for warm soil. Pinch flower-spikes off weekly to keep leaf production rolling.

feedingNotes: Light feeder; seaweed-and-fish liquid every 3 weeks.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Feb on heat mat. More heat-tolerant than sweet basil so it carries Papamoa harvests further into autumn under glass.

feedingNotes: Minimal feeding — too much nitrogen accelerates bolt. One seaweed-tea drench mid-cycle is plenty.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–May and Aug–Oct; skip the Papamoa peak summer or it bolts in 3 weeks. Direct-sow every fortnight for continuous leaf supply.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed. Liquid feed monthly through the productive months; biennial so will bolt in year two.
growingNotes: Sow Jul–Apr in Papamoa — almost year-round. Pre-soak seed 24 h to speed germination, and pick from outer stems first to keep the centre productive.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in spring; one liquid feed mid-season is plenty.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Apr from runners or cuttings. Always keep in a pot — Papamoa's mild winters mean it never dies back and will swallow a bed if let loose.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Top-up with compost in spring; liquid feed once per season after a hard cut-back.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Mar or divide existing clumps. In Papamoa they evergreen — cut to 3 cm twice a year to keep fresh, tender shoots coming.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in spring; one liquid feed after each cut-back.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Mar. Tougher than common chives and tolerates Papamoa summer humidity better — divide every 3 years to keep clumps vigorous.

feedingNotes: Light feeder; compost-rich bed plus one mid-season seaweed drench is enough.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Mar direct into the bed — taproots hate disturbance. In Papamoa it bolts fast in summer; succession-sow every 3 weeks for fresh foliage.

feedingNotes: Very low feeder; compost-mulch annually. Avoid liquid fertilisers — they dilute the oils.
greenhouseNotes: Perennial — cut back hard each spring.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Feb or buy plugs. Likes free-draining, slightly dry soil — Papamoa beds need to be raised or it sulks through wet winters.

feedingNotes: Avoid feeding. Annual compost mulch and free-draining soil are all it needs.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Feb or buy plugs; raised bed essential in Papamoa to prevent winter rot. Trim flowering stems back hard after blooming for bushier growth.

feedingNotes: Do not feed. Compost-mulch in early spring; lean soil yields the best aromatics.
growingNotes: Plant any time of year from a cutting or plug. Papamoa salt air suits it — give full sun and free-draining soil and prune lightly after flowering.

feedingNotes: Annual compost mulch only. Liquid feeds make leaves limp and reduce flavour oils.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Feb in trays or buy plugs. Replace plants every 4–5 years as old wood gets sparse — Papamoa humidity shortens its life vs drier climates.

feedingNotes: Light feeder; one spring compost mulch and an autumn cut-back is sufficient.
sowingNotes: Must be French tarragon — propagate by root division.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov from divisions only — seed-grown is Russian tarragon (no flavour). Lift and divide every 3 years to keep plants vigorous in Papamoa beds.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in spring; one liquid feed after a hard summer cut-back.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Feb. Like mint, contain in a pot — Papamoa's wet winters do not slow its spread. Cut back hard mid-summer for a fresh flush of clean leaves.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder for a herb. Compost + sheep pellets at planting; liquid feed monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant Oct–Dec from divisions in a frost-free greenhouse. In Papamoa it survives outdoors in a sheltered corner but greenhouse-grown stalks fatten faster.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Compost-rich bed; one seaweed drench mid-cycle.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–Apr and Aug–Oct — skip Papamoa summer or it bolts in 3 weeks. Likes light shade so tuck it under taller crops.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Compost-rich bed; liquid feed monthly through summer for vigorous leaf growth.
growingNotes: Sow Oct–Dec on heat mat. Frost-tender — keep in the Papamoa greenhouse year-round and harvest leaves before flower buds appear for peak sweetness.

feedingNotes: Light feeder; compost-rich bed plus monthly seaweed-and-fish liquid feed.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Dec on a heat mat (slow to germinate). Self-seeds enthusiastically — let one or two plants flower and Papamoa beds fill themselves next spring.

feedingNotes: Quick-cycle crop. Compost-rich bed plus weekly liquid feed for soft, tender leaves.
growingNotes: Sow every 2–3 weeks year-round in Papamoa. Use shade cloth Dec–Feb and choose heat-tolerant varieties or it bolts in midsummer.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed; weekly liquid feed for fast, sweet hearts.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–Oct in Papamoa — pause through Jan–Feb peak heat. Pick whole heads at 20 cm or treat as cut-and-come-again from outer leaves.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Compost-rich tray or bed; weekly liquid feed extends harvests.
growingNotes: Sow every 3 weeks year-round in Papamoa for continuous salad. Cut at 10 cm with scissors and plants regrow 2–3 times before bolting.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed plus weekly seaweed-and-fish liquid feed for dark, glossy leaves.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–Sep in Papamoa — it's a cool-season crop here. Pick outer leaves first or treat as cut-and-come-again to delay bolting.

feedingNotes: Tough plant — minimal feeding required. One compost mulch per year.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Mar; soak seed 24 h to break dormancy. Native to NZ coastlines so it thrives in Papamoa salt air and heat where ordinary spinach bolts.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed. Side-dress with sheep pellets every 2 months for steady year-round picking.
growingNotes: Sow year-round in Papamoa — one of the most reliable bed-fillers. Pick from outer leaves, leaving the centre to keep producing for 12+ months.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed; light liquid feed at the 4-leaf stage. Heavy nitrogen flattens flavour.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–Oct, every 3 weeks. Skip Papamoa peak summer — bolts within a fortnight in 25 °C+ heat. Pick outer leaves to keep plants productive longer.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed plus weekly liquid feed for fast, milder growth.
sowingNotes: Blanch the heart for milder leaves.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–Apr and Aug–Oct in Papamoa. Tie outer leaves over the heart 10 days before harvest to blanch — drier weather makes this cleaner.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed; light liquid feed at half-grown stage to encourage tight hearts.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–Apr and Aug–Oct. Cooler Papamoa autumn nights drive the red colouration — plants started in summer often stay green and bitter.

feedingNotes: Light liquid feed monthly. Too much fertiliser = soft leaves prone to rot.
sowingNotes: Constant moisture — pot stood in tray of water.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Apr in pots stood in a saucer of water. Papamoa tap water suits it; cut back hard every 8 weeks to refresh tender leaf production.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Compost-mulch in spring; liquid feed once after a hard cut-back.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Mar. Perennial in Papamoa — chop right back twice a year to refresh leaves and remove flower spikes before they set seed.

feedingNotes: Light feeder; compost-rich soil only. Liquid feeds make leaves limp.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–May and Aug–Oct. Cool-season crop; in Papamoa it's a key winter salad green and fills beds left empty by tomato season.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed; one mid-season liquid feed. Tolerant of poor soils once established.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Feb direct into warm soil. Thrives in Papamoa peak summer when other leafy greens bolt — pick young tips for stir-fries.

feedingNotes: None needed — seedling stored energy carries them through. Plain water is enough.
sowingNotes: Tray-grown — harvest at first true leaves.
growingNotes: Sow weekly year-round on a sunny windowsill or greenhouse bench. Papamoa winters are mild enough for unheated trays — harvest at 5–7 cm with scissors.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost + lime + sheep pellets pre-plant; liquid feed every 3 weeks.
growingNotes: Sow Jan–Apr and Jul–Sep. Long cropper in Papamoa — harvest from the bottom upwards and plants keep producing for 6+ months.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost + lime + sheep pellets pre-plant; liquid feed at 3-leaf and again at head-formation.
growingNotes: Sow Jan–Apr and Jul–Sep. Cut the main head at 15 cm and plants throw side-shoots for another 6–8 weeks of Papamoa harvest.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost + lime pre-plant; liquid feed every 3 weeks.
growingNotes: Sow Jan–Apr and Jul–Sep. Cut-and-come-again brassica — pick stems at 20 cm continuously and plants crop for 4 months in Papamoa.

feedingNotes: Very heavy feeder. Compost + lime + sheep pellets pre-plant; liquid feed every 2 weeks until heading.
growingNotes: Sow Jan–Mar and Jul–Aug. Tie outer leaves over forming heads to blanch them — Papamoa autumn drizzle stains exposed curds yellow.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost + lime + pellets pre-plant; liquid feed at 4-leaf and again at half-head.
growingNotes: Sow year-round in Papamoa. Match variety to season (summer types vs savoys) and net for white butterfly Sep–Apr — they will strip plants overnight.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost-rich bed; liquid feed weekly for fast, tight hearts.
growingNotes: Sow Jan–Apr and Aug–Oct. Bolts fast in Papamoa heat — keep cool with shade cloth and consistent water, and cover for white butterfly.

feedingNotes: Quick-cycle. Compost-rich soil + liquid feed at 2 weeks for tender stems.
growingNotes: Sow year-round in Papamoa, every 2–3 weeks for continuous supply. Net for white butterfly Sep–Apr; pick whole plants at 20 cm.

feedingNotes: Quick-cycle; compost-rich bed plus weekly liquid feed for tender stems.
growingNotes: Sow year-round, every 2 weeks for continuous Papamoa supply. Harvest the flowering stem just as buds form — that's the prime eating stage.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed plus weekly seaweed-and-fish liquid feed.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–Oct. Cool-season green — Papamoa autumn through spring is its prime window. Pick rosettes whole or cut leaves individually.

feedingNotes: Light feeder; compost-rich soil plus weekly liquid feed for steady growth.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–Oct, every 3 weeks. Cut-and-come-again — Papamoa's mild autumn extends harvests well into winter under glass.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed; weekly liquid feed for milder, larger leaves.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–Oct. Cooler Papamoa weather develops the warmest mustard heat — summer growth is fast but flavour is bland.

feedingNotes: Compost + lime pre-plant; liquid feed at 3-leaf stage and once bulbs start swelling.
growingNotes: Sow Jan–Apr and Aug–Oct in Papamoa. Harvest at tennis-ball size — left longer they go woody. Net for white butterfly through summer.

feedingNotes: Heavy long-season feeder. Compost + lime + pellets pre-plant; liquid feed monthly through summer.
sowingNotes: Long season grower — needs full sun.
growingNotes: Sow Oct–Jan; plant out in well-firmed soil and stake — Papamoa wind rocks loose plants. Pick from bottom upwards once sprouts hit walnut size.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Compost-rich bed only — high nitrogen pushes leaf at the cost of root.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–Oct direct in Papamoa. Harvest at golf-ball size for sweetness; left longer they go woody and bitter.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed. One light liquid feed at half-grown stage; hold off nitrogen later or roots split.
growingNotes: Sow Nov–Feb direct. Slow Papamoa winter crop — harvest from late autumn after the first cool snap sweetens the flesh.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed only. Avoid extra nitrogen — encourages leaf at cost of root.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–May and Aug–Oct direct into deep, stone-free Papamoa soil. Harvest at 30 cm long; bolts fast in heat so avoid mid-summer sowing.

feedingNotes: Almost no feeding. Compost-rich soil only — extra fertiliser produces leafy plants and woody roots.
sowingNotes: Fastest crop in the garden — direct sow.
growingNotes: Sow direct year-round in Papamoa, every fortnight for continuous picking. Harvest at 3 cm — left in the ground past 6 weeks they go pithy and hot.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Avoid fresh manure — it forks the roots. One mid-season liquid feed if leaves yellow.
sowingNotes: Don't transplant — direct sow into deep, stone-free soil.
growingNotes: Sow direct year-round in Papamoa; thinning is key — overcrowded carrots stay matchstick-thin. Net to deter carrot fly through summer.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed; one liquid feed at half-grown stage. Tolerates sandy Papamoa soil if mulched.
growingNotes: Sow year-round in Papamoa, every 4 weeks. Harvest at tennis-ball size for sweetness; thin clusters to single plants for proper bulbs.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. No fresh manure — forks roots. One mid-season seaweed drench is plenty.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Mar direct into deep, stone-free soil. Slow to germinate (3–4 weeks) — mark rows and keep moist. Sweetens after first Papamoa cool snap.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost-rich bed; liquid feed every 3 weeks through the long growing season.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Oct on heat mat. Long Papamoa season suits it — strip lower leaves as bulbs swell to expose them and improve final size.

feedingNotes: Compost + sheep pellets in trench at planting; one liquid feed at flowering. Avoid lime — likes slightly acidic soil.
growingNotes: Plant Jul–Dec; mound soil over stems as they grow to prevent green tubers. Papamoa frost-free start lets you crop earlies by Nov.

feedingNotes: Light feeder; too much nitrogen pushes leaf at cost of tubers. Compost-rich bed only.
growingNotes: Plant Oct–Dec slips into warm, sandy Papamoa soil. Lift vines off the bed weekly to stop them rooting where they trail; harvest before the first cool autumn rain.

feedingNotes: Compost at planting; no further feeding required.
sowingNotes: Harvest after first frost knocks back foliage.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov tubers. Tubers form only after autumn equinox — patience pays. Papamoa winters knock the foliage back; lift right after.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in spring — that's it. Tough perennial, almost weed-tough.
growingNotes: Plant Aug–Oct in a contained bed or large tub — left loose in Papamoa beds it spreads aggressively. Harvest after foliage dies back in autumn.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in spring; no liquid feeds needed.
greenhouseNotes: Contain in pot or it will take over.
growingNotes: Plant Aug–Oct root cuttings in a buried pot — Papamoa beds it will overrun in two years if planted loose. Lift roots in winter and replant a thumb-sized piece.

feedingNotes: Compost + lime pre-plant; liquid feed monthly until tops start to fall. Then stop watering and feeding to cure bulbs.
growingNotes: Sow Mar–Jul, plant out Apr–Aug. Match variety to Papamoa daylength (long-day NZ types). Bend tops over once 50% have flopped to speed curing.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Compost-rich bed plus liquid feed every 4 weeks for thicker stems.
growingNotes: Sow year-round in Papamoa, every 6 weeks. Pull whole plants at pencil-width or treat as cut-and-come-again, leaving 3 cm of base to regrow.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed; liquid feed every 3 weeks through summer growth.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Dec; transplant into 15 cm holes and water in (don't fill the hole) to blanch the white shaft. Long Papamoa autumn perfect for slow finish.

feedingNotes: Compost + lime pre-plant; one liquid feed at 6 weeks then stop to cure.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug; each bulb multiplies into a clump of 6–10. Lift when tops yellow and dry on a Papamoa sunny rack for 2 weeks before storing.

feedingNotes: Compost + lime + sheep pellets pre-plant; liquid feed monthly Aug–Oct then stop to cure bulbs.
sowingNotes: Plant cloves on the shortest day; harvest on the longest.
growingNotes: Plant cloves on the shortest day (21 Jun) and harvest near the longest (21 Dec). Papamoa winters give just enough chill for proper bulb division.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder for an allium. Compost + pellets pre-plant; liquid feed monthly Aug–Oct.
growingNotes: Plant May–Jul. Mild flavour, fist-sized bulbs — mulch heavily through Papamoa winter and remove flower scapes in spring to push energy into bulbs.

feedingNotes: Light feeder — fixes own nitrogen. One compost mulch and a phosphorus-rich (bone meal) pre-plant feed only.
growingNotes: Sow Mar–Sep direct. Cool-season crop in Papamoa — bolts in summer heat. Pick pods every 2–3 days to keep plants producing.

feedingNotes: Self-feeds nitrogen. Compost + bone-meal pre-plant; no further fertiliser needed.
growingNotes: Sow Mar–Sep direct on a 1.8 m trellis. Pick flat pods every other day in Papamoa or they go fibrous overnight in warm weather.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Compost + bone-meal pre-plant; no extra nitrogen.
growingNotes: Sow Mar–Sep direct on a tall trellis. Pick pods plump but before peas swell hard. Papamoa autumn-spring is its prime window.

feedingNotes: Self-feeds nitrogen. Compost + bone-meal pre-plant; one liquid feed at flowering.
growingNotes: Sow Mar–Jul direct. Pinch growing tips once 6 trusses set to deter blackfly and push pod-fill — a Papamoa winter staple.

feedingNotes: Self-feeds nitrogen. Compost-rich bed; one liquid feed at flowering.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Feb direct into warm soil. Two block plantings 4 weeks apart give continuous pods through Papamoa summer. Pick every 2 days.

feedingNotes: Compost + bone-meal pre-plant; one liquid feed at flowering. Avoid extra nitrogen.
greenhouseNotes: Trellis to roof — keep tips pinched.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Jan direct alongside a 2 m trellis or wigwam. Long-cropping in Papamoa — pods continue Dec–May provided you pick every 2 days.

feedingNotes: Self-feeds nitrogen. Compost + potash-rich feed at flowering for full pods.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Dec direct against a tall wigwam. Mist flowers in Papamoa peak summer — high heat without humidity prevents pod-set.

feedingNotes: Self-feeds nitrogen. Compost-rich bed only.
growingNotes: Sow Oct–Dec direct into warm Papamoa soil. Pick whole plants when pods are plump and bright green — they all mature within a week.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost + sheep pellets at planting; liquid feed at knee-high and again at tasseling.
growingNotes: Sow Sep–Dec in a block 4 wide × 4 deep — wind-pollinated and patches don't fill on row plantings. Pick when silks brown and kernels milk.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost-rich bed; liquid feed every 2 weeks through summer.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Oct, plant out Sep–Nov. Constant moisture is non-negotiable in Papamoa heat — mulch heavily and water daily through Dec–Feb.

feedingNotes: Compost-rich bed; one liquid feed at half-grown stage. Avoid water stress — bulbs split.
growingNotes: Sow Feb–Apr and Aug–Sep. Bolts in Papamoa midsummer — autumn sowings give the cleanest, fattest bulbs. Mulch around the base to keep moisture even.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost + sheep pellets in autumn; liquid feed monthly through cropping season.
sowingNotes: Plant crowns; don't harvest the first year.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug crowns. First year: let it establish, no picking. From year 2 in Papamoa it crops Sep–Jan; remove flower stalks immediately to keep stems coming.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost + bone meal in autumn; liquid feed monthly through ferning season.
sowingNotes: Plant crowns; wait 2–3 years before first harvest.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug crowns in a permanent bed. No picking year 1–2; light pick year 3. In Papamoa cut the ferns down once they yellow each autumn to expose crowns to winter chill.

feedingNotes: Compost + sheep pellets in autumn; liquid feed monthly through spring and summer.
growingNotes: Sow Aug–Oct. Each plant produces 6–10 buds in year 2 — pick when scales are tight. Cut foliage to ground after harvest in Papamoa to refresh.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets at planting; liquid feed monthly through summer leaf growth.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov rhizomes 5 cm deep in a Papamoa greenhouse — too cold outside year-round. Lift in winter once foliage dies back; replant a thumb piece for next season.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets at planting; monthly liquid feed through leaf-growth season.
greenhouseNotes: Greenhouse only — needs long warm season.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov rhizomes in greenhouse pots. Needs the full Papamoa summer under cover; lift in winter and store unwashed in dry sand for replanting.

feedingNotes: Compost + potash pre-plant; liquid potash feed weekly once flowering. Switch to half-strength after main flush.
sowingNotes: Plant runners; everbearers fruit through summer.
growingNotes: Plant May–Aug runners into well-mulched beds. Net for blackbirds before fruit colour up. Replace plants every 3 years in Papamoa to dodge virus build-up.

feedingNotes: Citrus food in Aug + Feb; compost tea fortnightly Oct–Mar. Magnesium spray once a year if leaves yellow.
growingNotes: Plant any time in a 40 L pot of citrus mix. Papamoa coastal warmth suits Meyer perfectly — fruits year-round and tolerates the salt air outdoors in a sheltered spot.

feedingNotes: Citrus food Aug + Feb; compost tea monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in 40 L pot. More frost-tender than lemons — keep in the Papamoa greenhouse Jun–Aug or wheel pots out only during the day.

feedingNotes: Citrus food twice a year; compost tea monthly Oct–Mar.
greenhouseNotes: Grown for leaves more than fruit.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in 30 L pot. Grown mainly for the aromatic leaves in Papamoa — pinch tips regularly to push leaf production over fruit.

feedingNotes: Citrus food Aug + Feb; compost tea monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant any time in 30 L pot. Hardiest citrus — easy in a Papamoa garden corner. Pick fruit whole; thin skin is sweet, flesh is tart.

feedingNotes: Citrus food Aug + Feb; compost tea monthly Oct–Mar.
greenhouseNotes: Sour, ornamental — used in marmalade and dressings.
growingNotes: Plant any time in 30 L pot. Almost continuous fruit and flower in Papamoa coastal warmth — ornamental as well as productive.

feedingNotes: Citrus food Aug + Feb; compost tea monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in 40 L pot. Cool Papamoa autumn nights drive the colour change in May; harvest as soon as fruit feels heavy for size.

feedingNotes: Citrus food Aug + Feb; compost tea monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in 40 L pot. Thin fruit clusters to one per cluster in Dec for larger Papamoa harvest the following winter.

feedingNotes: Citrus food Aug + Feb; compost tea monthly Oct–Mar; magnesium sulphate yearly.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in 50 L pot or sheltered Papamoa garden corner. Seedless, easy peel — cropping mid-winter when other citrus is finishing.

feedingNotes: Citrus food Aug + Feb; compost tea monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in 50 L pot. Long ripening period — leave fruit on tree as long as possible; flavour deepens. Papamoa winter sun does the work.

feedingNotes: Citrus food twice a year; compost tea monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov. Cold-tolerant citrus, perfect for Papamoa — zest and juice both used. Mind the spines when pruning.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in Aug; one liquid feed at fruit-set. Avoid rich fertiliser — pushes leaf at cost of fruit.
pruningNotes: Prune to 4 main stems in winter.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. In Papamoa it gives a breba crop in Dec and a main crop in Mar — net for birds before colour change.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in Aug; one liquid feed at fruit-set.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug. Stays under 1.5 m so suits Papamoa courtyards in a 20 L pot. Crops twice yearly in our climate.

feedingNotes: Compost + sheep pellets in Aug; liquid feed at flowering and fruit-set.
greenhouseNotes: Move outdoors Jun–Aug for chill, return for flowering.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root in 40 L pot. Spray copper at leaf-fall and again at bud-swell to prevent leaf curl — Papamoa humidity makes this non-negotiable.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed at flowering and fruit-set.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. Copper-spray at leaf-fall in Papamoa or leaf curl will defoliate the tree by Sep. Thin fruit to one per 10 cm of branch.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed at flowering and fruit-set.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root in 30 L pot — stays under 1.8 m. Copper-spray twice a year in Papamoa to prevent leaf curl. Net for birds in Dec.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed at flowering and fruit-set.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. Copper-spray at leaf-fall and bud-swell against leaf curl. Thin fruit to one per 10 cm to size up fruit in Papamoa.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed at flowering and fruit-set.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. Low chill suits Papamoa winters perfectly. Copper-spray at leaf-fall and bud-swell; thin fruit at marble size.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed at flowering and fruit-set.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. One of the few apricots that fruits reliably in Papamoa's mild winters. Net for birds — they hit ripening apricots fast.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; one liquid feed at fruit-set.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. Sour Morello-type — best for Papamoa as sweet cherries need more winter chill than we get. Self-fertile in pots.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed at flowering.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root in 40 L pot. Self-fertile — single tree crops well. Thin fruit at marble size to prevent branch breakage and size up fruit.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed at flowering. Boron added once a year.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. Self-fertile dwarf, stays under 1.5 m — fits a Papamoa back yard. Net for birds; harvest when hulls split open.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed monthly Sep–Dec.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root in 40 L pot. Low-chill variety suited to Papamoa winters. Thin fruit clusters to one apple at marble size for size and quality.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed monthly Sep–Dec.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. Compact tree fits a Papamoa courtyard pot. Mini apples ripen May; net early for birds.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in Aug; one mid-spring liquid feed.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. Self-fertile and tough — handles Papamoa coastal wind once established. Plant away from paths; ripe fruit stains everything.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Sep; liquid feed monthly through summer.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov. Suits Papamoa — coastal warmth and drier autumns drive fruit colour. Reduce water at ripening to prevent skin splitting.

feedingNotes: Compost + sheep pellets in Aug; liquid feed monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant Apr–Oct in 40 L pot or sheltered Papamoa garden. Pick fruit from the ground daily once they start dropping — they only ripen off the tree.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Sep; liquid feed monthly through summer.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in greenhouse pot — Papamoa winter outdoors is borderline frost-risk. Pinch tips after flowering to encourage bushy growth.

feedingNotes: Light feeder. Compost-mulch in Sep; one slow-release pellet application annually.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in 40 L pot — Papamoa coastal warmth and salt air suit it. Prune lightly after harvest to keep an open vase shape and encourage next year's wood.

feedingNotes: Compost + zinc/boron + sulphate of ammonia in Sep; liquid feed monthly through summer.
greenhouseNotes: Grow in greenhouse for early years.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in 50 L pot; keep under cover in Papamoa for the first 3 winters. Self-fertile dwarf but a second tree (different flower type) lifts yields.

feedingNotes: Low-phosphorus feeder — Proteaceae sensitive. Compost-mulch only; avoid standard NPK fertilisers.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in 50 L pot. Slow grower in Papamoa — 6 years to first crop. Pick nuts off the ground; they ripen and drop on their own.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Sep; liquid feed monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in sheltered Papamoa spot or 40 L pot. Brittle wood — stake well against coastal wind. Replace plants every 5 years as production drops.

feedingNotes: Heavy feeder. Compost + pellets in Sep + Dec; liquid feed every 2 weeks Oct–Apr.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Dec in 50 L pot or greenhouse. Each stem fruits once then dies — let one sucker grow on for next year's crop. Papamoa frost-free corners outdoors work too.

feedingNotes: Acidic-loving plant food in spring; compost-mulch monthly. Avoid lime.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Dec in 30 L pot; keep in the Papamoa greenhouse year-round — frost-tender. Pick cherries when bright red; expect tiny harvests as a novelty crop.

feedingNotes: Acidic ericaceous fertiliser in Aug + Nov. No lime, no standard NPK — kills feeder roots.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug in 30 L pot of acidic ericaceous mix — Papamoa soil is too alkaline straight. Net for birds Dec–Feb; mulch with pine bark to keep pH down.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root in 30 L pot. Thornless and compact — fits Papamoa decks and balconies. Cut fruited canes to ground after harvest.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in Aug; liquid feed monthly Oct–Feb.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root and trellis along a 2 m wire fence. Cut fruited canes to ground after harvest; Papamoa heat dries new canes fast — mulch heavily.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in Aug; liquid feed monthly Oct–Jan.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root on a sturdy 2 m trellis. Tie new canes in a fan shape; cut fruited canes to ground after picking. Papamoa coast suits it.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in Aug; liquid feed monthly Oct–Jan.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root and trellis. Trains and fruits like a boysenberry; cut fruited canes to ground after picking. Tart fruit, great for cooking.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in Aug; one liquid feed at flowering.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. Cool-climate plant — Papamoa is borderline; best in light afternoon shade. Net for birds and prune to an open goblet shape.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in Aug; liquid feed once at fruit-set.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. Likes Papamoa winter chill but needs afternoon shade in summer to prevent leaf scorch. Net for birds before fruit colours.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed at fruit-set.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root. Cooler-climate plant — Papamoa is borderline. Cut a third of old wood to ground each winter to keep new fruiting wood coming.

feedingNotes: Acidic ericaceous food only. Avoid lime and standard NPK fertilisers.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug in 30 L pot of acidic peat-based mix. Stand pot in a tray of water through Papamoa summer — never lets dry. Pick fruit Apr–Jun.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in Aug; one liquid feed at fruit-set. Tough plant — overfeeding reduces fruiting.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov in 30 L pot or sheltered garden corner. Tough and tolerates Papamoa salt air; prune hard in winter to keep manageable as it suckers freely.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Sep; liquid feed monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov against a sturdy 2 m trellis. Papamoa coastal warmth gives heavy crops; replace vines every 5 years as woodiness slows production.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Sep; liquid feed monthly Oct–Mar.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov on tall trellis. More heat-loving than 'Black' — ideal for Papamoa greenhouse or warmest garden corner. Pick fruit from the ground daily once dropping.

feedingNotes: Compost + pellets in Aug; liquid feed monthly Oct–Mar; lime every 2 years.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root on a strong pergola. Need both male (Tomuri) and female (Hayward) within 5 m for pollination. Cut spent fruiting laterals back hard each winter.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in Aug; one liquid feed at fruit-set. Avoid heavy nitrogen — pushes leaf at cost of grapes.
growingNotes: Plant Jun–Aug bare-root on a Papamoa greenhouse roof or pergola. Spur-prune each winter to one bud per spur; thin bunches at pea size to size up berries.

feedingNotes: Cactus-and-succulent fertiliser in Sep + Dec; minimal water-soluble feed. Avoid heavy nitrogen.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov from a cutting against a sturdy post topped with a 'crown' for the cactus to drape over. Frost-free Papamoa greenhouse only — pollinate flowers by hand at dusk.

feedingNotes: Compost-mulch in Sep; light liquid feed monthly through summer leaf growth.
greenhouseNotes: Pot, top-rooted from a fresh fruit crown.
growingNotes: Plant Sep–Nov from a fresh crown twisted off a supermarket pineapple — root in dry sand 2 weeks first. Frost-free Papamoa greenhouse only; one fruit per plant after 2–3 years.
